title: Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport
claim: A standard spectral model with a small retained-mode budget drifts and distorts under autoregressive rollout; more modes reduce this error.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend on top, error value in titles
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a title, 'Autoregressive rollout: predicted vs. ground-truth final state', and a legend at the top. The legend shows a solid black line for ground truth and a dashed red line for the FNO prediction. The left panel is FNO with 8 modes and relative error 2.51e+00. Its red curve oscillates wildly between about -2 and 2.4, with phase shifts, amplitude distortion and spurious ripples in flat regions. The right panel is FNO with 20 modes and relative error 3.20e-01. Its red curve follows the black ground-truth waveform of two smooth bumps and a sharp edge, with only small residual wiggles. The y-axis is u(x,T). The eye goes first to the large red oscillations on the left, then to the close match on the right.
caption: Autoregressive rollout on the PDEBench 1D advection benchmark [ref]. Both FNOs are trained as one-step predictors and differ only in the number of retained Fourier modes. A small mode budget leads to phase drift, amplitude distortion, and oscillatory artifacts, while increasing the number of modes improves the final-state prediction.
abstract: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity. We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.
